entries.ef0564a0e4ffb2c9d33ae70d933ab309bbe39633: <div sID="gen12977" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="125" osisID="Ps.125" sID="Ps.125"/> <div eID="gen12977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12978" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12979" type="x-p"/> This short psalm may be summed up in those words of the prophet (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.10-Isa.3.11">Isa. iii. 10, 11</reference>), "Say you to the righteous, It shall be well with him. Woe to the wicked, it shall be ill with him." Thus are life and death, the blessing and the curse, set before us often in the psalms, as well as in the law and the prophets. I. It is certainly well with the people of God; for, 1. They have the promises of a good God that they shall be fixed (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.1">ver. 1</reference>), and safe (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">ver. 2</reference>), and not always under the hatches, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.3">ver. 3</reference>. 2. They have the prayers of a good man, which shall be heard for them, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.4">ver. 4</reference>. II. It is certainly ill with the wicked, and particularly with the apostates, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.5">ver. 5</reference>. Some of the Jewish rabbies are of opinion that it has reference to the days of the Messiah; however, we that are members of the gospel-church may certainly, in singing this psalm, take comfort of these promises, and the more so if we stand in awe of the threatening.
entries.49195ad377b4994eda16bfd644f3da9419c5528b: <div eID="gen12979" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12978" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Security of God's People.</title> <div sID="gen12980" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> They that trust in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> as mount Zion, <hi type="italic">which</hi> cannot be removed, <hi type="italic">but</hi> abideth for ever. <hi type="super">2</hi> As the mountains <hi type="italic">are</hi> round about Jerusalem, so the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> round about his people from henceforth even for ever. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous; lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity. <div eID="gen12980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12981" type="x-p"/> Here are three very precious promises made to the people of God, which, though they are designed to secure the welfare of the church in general, may be applied by particular believers to themselves, as other promises of this nature may. Here is, <div eID="gen12981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12982" type="x-p"/> I. The character of God's people, to whom these promises belong. Many call themselves God's people who have no part nor lot in this matter. But those shall have the benefit of them and may take the comfort of them, (1.) Who are <hi type="italic">righteous</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.3">v. 3</reference>), righteous before God, righteous to God, and righteous to all men, for his sake justified and sanctified. (2.) Who <hi type="italic">trust in the Lord,</hi> who depend upon his care and devote themselves to his honour. All that deal with God must deal upon trust, and he will give comfort to those only that give credit to him, and make it to appear they do so by quitting other confidences, and venturing to the utmost for God. The closer our expectations are confined to God the higher our expectations may be raised from him. <div eID="gen12982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12983" type="x-p"/> II. The promises themselves. <div eID="gen12983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12984" type="x-p"/> 1. That their hearts shall be established by faith: those minds shall be truly stayed that are stayed on God: <hi type="italic">They shall be as Mount Zion.</hi> The church in general is called <hi type="italic">Mount Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">Heb. xii. 22</reference>), and it shall in <hi type="italic">this</hi> respect be like <hi type="italic">Mount Zion,</hi> it shall be built upon a rock, and its interests shall be so well secured that <hi type="italic">the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.</hi> The stability of the church is the satisfaction of all its well-wishers. Particular persons, who trust in God, shall be established (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.7">Ps. cxii. 7</reference>); their faith shall be their fixation, <reference osisRef="Isa.7.9">Isa. vii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall be as Mount Zion,</hi> which is firm as it is a mountain supported by providence, much more as a holy mountain supported by promise. (1.) They <hi type="italic">cannot be removed</hi> by the prince of the power of the air, nor by all his subtlety and strength. They cannot be removed from their integrity nor from their confidence in God. (2.) They <hi type="italic">abide for ever</hi> in that grace which is the earnest of their everlasting continuance in glory. <div eID="gen12984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12985" type="x-p"/> 2. That, committing themselves to God, they shall be safe, under his protection, from all the insults of their enemies, as Jerusalem had a natural fastness and fortification in the <hi type="italic">mountains</hi> that <hi type="italic">were round about it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">v. 2</reference>. Those mountains not only sheltered it from winds and tempests, and broke the force of them, but made it also very difficult of access for an enemy; such a defence is God's providence to his people. Observe, (1.) The compass of it: <hi type="italic">The Lord is round about his people</hi> on every side. There is no gap in the hedge of protection which he makes round about his people, at which the enemy, who goes about them, seeking to do them a mischief, can find entrance, <reference osisRef="Job.1.10">Job i. 10</reference>. (2.) The continuance of it—<hi type="italic">henceforth even for ever.</hi> Mountains may moulder and <hi type="italic">come to nought, and rocks</hi> be <hi type="italic">removed out of their place</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.14.18">Job xiv. 18</reference>), but God's covenant with his people cannot be <hi type="italic">broken</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.10">Isa. liv. 10</reference>) nor his care of them cease. Their being said to stand fast <hi type="italic">for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.1">v. 1</reference>), and here to have God <hi type="italic">round about them for ever,</hi> intimates that the promises of the stability and security of God's people will have their full accomplishment in their everlasting state. In heaven they shall <hi type="italic">stand fast for ever,</hi> shall be as <hi type="italic">pillars in the temple of our God and go no more out</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Rev. iii. 12</reference>), and there God himself, with his glory and favour, will be <hi type="italic">round about them for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen12985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12986" type="x-p"/> 3. That their troubles shall last no longer than their strength will serve to bear them up under them, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.3">v. 3</reference>. (1.) It is supposed that the <hi type="italic">rod of the wicked</hi> may come, may fall, <hi type="italic">upon the lot of the righteous.</hi> The rod of their power may oppress them; the rod of their anger may vex and torment them. It may fall upon their persons, their estates, their liberties, their families, their names, any thing that falls to their lot, only it cannot reach their souls. (2.) It is promised that, though it may come upon their lot, it shall not rest there; it shall not continue so long as the enemies design, and as the people of God fear, but God will cut the work short in righteousness, so short that even <hi type="italic">with the temptation he will make a way for them to escape.</hi> (3.) It is considered as a reason of this promise that if the trouble should continue over-long the righteous themselves would be in temptation to <hi type="italic">put forth their hands to iniquity,</hi> to join with wicked people in their wicked practices, to say as they say and do as they do. There is danger lest, being long persecuted for their religion, at length they grow weary of it and willing to give it up, lest, being kept long in expectation of promised mercies, they begin to distrust the promise, and to think of casting God off, upon suspicion of his having cast them off. See <reference osisRef="Ps.73.13-Ps.73.14">Ps. lxxiii. 13, 14</reference>. Note, God considers the frame of his people, and will proportion their trials to their strength by the care of his providence, as well as their strength to their trials by the power of his grace. <hi type="italic">Oppression makes a wise man mad,</hi> especially if it continue long; therefore <hi type="italic">for the elect's sake</hi> the days shall be shortened, that, whatever becomes of their lot in this world, they may not lose their lot among the chosen.
entries.b14a4e8ad07eea93024f91dd5aa5e37246e426a3: <div eID="gen12986" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Security of God's People.</title> <div sID="gen12987" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Do good, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , unto <hi type="italic">those that be</hi> good, and <hi type="italic">to them that are</hi> upright in their hearts. <hi type="super">5</hi> As for such as turn aside unto their crooked ways, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall lead them forth with the workers of iniquity: <hi type="italic">but</hi> peace <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon Israel. <div eID="gen12987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12988" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The prayer the psalmist puts up for the happiness of those that are sincere and constant (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Do good, O Lord! unto those that are good.</hi> This teaches us to pray for all good people, to <hi type="italic">make supplication for all saints;</hi> and we may pray in faith for them, being assured that those who do well shall certainly be well dealt with. Those that are as they should be shall be as they would be, provided they be <hi type="italic">upright in heart,</hi> that they be really as good as they seem to be. <hi type="italic">With the upright God will show himself upright.</hi> He does not say, Do good, O Lord! to those that are perfect, that are sinless and spotless, but to those that are sincere and honest. God's promises should quicken our prayers. It is comfortable wishing well to those for whom God has engaged to do well. 2. The prospect he has of the ruin of hypocrites and deserters; he does not pray for it (<hi type="italic">I have not desired the woeful day, thou knowest</hi>), but he predicts it: <hi type="italic">As for those,</hi> who having known the way of righteousness, for fear of the rod of the wicked, basely turn aside out of it <hi type="italic">to their wicked ways,</hi> use indirect ways to prevent trouble or extricate themselves out of it, or those who, instead of reforming, grow worse and worse and are more obstinate and daring in their impieties, God shall <hi type="italic">send them away, cast them out,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lead them forth with the workers of iniquity,</hi> that is, he will appoint them their portion with the worst of sinners. Note, (1.) Sinful ways are <hi type="italic">crooked ways;</hi> sin is the perverting of that which is right. (2.) The doom of those who turn aside to those crooked ways out of the right way will be the same with theirs who have all along walked in them, nay, and more grievous, for if any place in hell be hotter than another that shall be the portion of hypocrites and apostates. God shall <hi type="italic">lead them forth,</hi> as prisoners are led forth to execution. <hi type="italic">Go, you cursed, into everlasting fire;</hi> and <hi type="italic">these shall go away;</hi> all their former righteousness shall not be mentioned unto them. The last words, <hi type="italic">Peace upon Israel,</hi> may be taken as a prayer: "God preserve his Israel in peace, when his judgments are abroad reckoning with evil-doers." We read them as a promise: <hi type="italic">Peace shall be upon Israel;</hi> that is, [1.] When those who have treacherously deserted the ways of God meet with their own destruction those who faithfully adhere to them, though they may have trouble in their way, shall have peace in the end. [2.] The destruction of those who walk in crooked ways will contribute to the peace and safety of the church. When Herod was cut off <hi type="italic">the word of God grew,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.12.23-Acts.12.24">Acts xii. 23, 24</reference>. [3.] The peace and happiness of God's Israel will be the vexation, and will add much to the torment, of those who perish in their wickedness, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.28">Luke xiii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.13">Isa. lxv. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">My servants shall rejoice, but you shall be ashamed.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.125"/> <div eID="gen12988" type="x-p"/>

entries.35347fd0d2f3bbb2a8d92a1e8cd07796e9efebac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7010"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 125</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.125.1-Ps.125.5">Psa 125:1-5</reference>. God honors the confidence of His people, by protection and deliverance, and leaves hypocrites to the doom of the wicked.</title> <div sID="gen10756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7010"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Mount Zion--</hi>as an emblem of permanence, and locality of Jerusalem as one of security, represent the firm and protected condition of God's people (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.46.5">Psa 46:5</reference>), supported not only by Providence, but by covenant promise. Even the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed, but God's kindness shall not depart, nor His covenant of peace be removed (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.10">Is 54:10</reference>).<div eID="gen10756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10757" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They that trust--</hi>are "His people," (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10757" type="x-p"/>
entries.12a1be75f67a332f1e0f8bed8cbc03f977398e26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7011"/><div sID="gen10758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7011"/>3. Though God may leave them for a time under the "rod," or power (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.9">Psa 2:9</reference>), and oppression of the wicked for a time, as a chastisement, He will not suffer them to be tempted so as to fall into sin (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1Co 10:13</reference>). The wicked shall only prove a correcting rod to them, not a destroying sword; even this rod shall not remain ("rest") on them, lest they be tempted to despair and apostasy (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.13">Psa 73:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">14</reference>). God may even try His people to the uttermost: when nothing is before our eyes but pure despair, then He delivers us and gives life in death, and makes us blessed in the curse (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.8">2Co 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>) [Luther].<div eID="gen10758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the lot--</hi>the possession, literally, "Canaan," spiritually, the heavenly inheritance of holiness and bliss which is appointed to the righteous. Sin's dominion shall not permanently come between the believer and his inheritance. <div eID="gen10759" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5c6d1113c427967b00d800d940f1fa1839eaa70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7012"/><div sID="gen10760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7012"/>4. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">84:11</reference>). <div eID="gen10760" type="x-p"/>
entries.8dddef1653bb81aeb1a01ff931298e463b1b1e0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7013"/><div sID="gen10761" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7013"/>5. Those who turn aside (under temptation) permanently show that they are hypocrites, and their lot or portion shall be with the wicked (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">Psa 28:3</reference>).<div eID="gen10761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crooked ways--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.9.16">De 9:16</reference>; Mal <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2:8, 9</reference>).<div eID="gen10762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their--</hi>is emphatic; the "crooked ways" proceed from their own hearts. The true Israel is here distinguished from the false. Scripture everywhere opposes the Jewish delusion that mere outward descent would save (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.28">Ro 2:28</reference>, 29; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.6">9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.6.16">Ga 6:16</reference>). The byways of sin from the way of life. <chapter eID="Ps.125"/>

entries.b401e4ab392fa842ab899dbd493f94caab670626: <div eID="gen23064" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23065" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23066" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23066" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23065" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23067" type="x-p"/> The safety of those who trust in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.125.1">Psa 125:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference>. God's protecting providence in behalf of his followers, <reference osisRef="Psa.125.3">Psa 125:3</reference>. A prayer for the godly, <reference osisRef="Psa.125.4">Psa 125:4</reference>. The evil lot of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Psa.125.5">Psa 125:5</reference>. <div eID="gen23067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23068" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is without a title: it belongs most probably to the times after the captivity; and has been applied, with apparent propriety, to the opposition which Sanballat the Horonite, Geshem the Arabian, and Tobiah the Ammonite, gave to the Jews while employed in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem, and restoring the temple. <div eID="gen23068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23069" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23070" type="x-p"/> They that trust in the Lord - Every faithful Jew who confides in Jehovah shall stand, in those open and secret attacks of the enemies of God and truth, as unshaken as Mount Zion; and shall not be moved by the power of any adversary.
entries.72d814db86f2d95fc1b2a3f77326bfb197b9ee2d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23071" type="x-p"/> As the mountains are round about Jerusalem - Jerusalem, according to Sandys, was situated on a rocky mountain every way to be ascended, except a little on the north, with steep ascents and deep valleys, naturally fortified. It is surrounded with other mountains, at no great distance, as if placed in the midst of an amphitheatre; for on the east is Mount Olivet, separated from the city by the valley of Jehoshaphat, which also encompasses a part of the north; on the south, the mountain of Offiner interposed with the valley of Gehinnom; and on the west it was formerly fenced with the valley of Gihon, and the mountains adjoining. The situation was such as to be easily rendered impregnable. <div eID="gen23071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23072" type="x-p"/> The Lord is round about his people - He is above, beneath, around them; and while they keep within it, their fortress is impregnable, and they can suffer no evil.
entries.ff3674c19d696b9ae87543947036a5e25da96623: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23073" type="x-p"/> For the rod of the worked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous - Rod, here. may be taken for persecution, or for rule; and then it may be thus interpreted: "The wicked shall not be permitted to persecute always, nor to have a permanent rule." In our liturgic version this clause is thus rendered: "The rod of the ungodly cometh not into the lot of the righteous." "This," said one of our forefathers, "is neither truth nor scripture. First, it is not truth; for the rod of the wicked doth come into the inheritance of the righteous, and that often. Secondly, it is not scripture, for the text saith, 'The rod of the wicked shall not rest there.' It may come, and stay for a time; but it shall not be permitted to abide." This is only one, and not the worst, of the many sad blemishes which deform the Version in our national Prayer-book. In short, the Version of the Psalms in that book is wholly unworthy of regard; and should be thrown aside, and that in the authorized Version in the Bible substituted for it. The people of God are misled by it; and they are confounded with the great and glaring differences they find between it and what they findd in their Bibles, where they have a version of a much better character, delivered to them by the authority of Church and state. Why do not our present excellent and learned prelates lay this to heart, and take away this sore stumbling-block out of the way of the people? I have referred to this subject in the introduction to the Book of Psalms. <div eID="gen23073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23074" type="x-p"/> Lest the righteous put forth - Were the wicked to bear rule in the Lord's vineyard, religion would soon become extinct; for the great mass of the people would conform to their rulers. Fear not your enemies, while ye fear God. Neither Sanballat, nor Tobiah, nor Geshem, nor any of God's foes, shall be able to set up their rod, their power and authority, here. While you are faithful, the Lord will laugh them to scorn.
entries.3a68cd6a98ffbb6da7ab28f7d8326c3bb4bdfe36: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23075" type="x-p"/> Do good, O Lord, unto those that be good - Let the upright ever find thee his sure defense! Increase the goodness which thou hast already bestowed upon them; and let all who are upright in heart find thee to be their stay and their support!
entries.84cf977503ea9e1ac0cb374b16c851900e21d96f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23076" type="x-p"/> As for such as turn aside - Who are not faithful; who give way to sin; who backslide, and walk in a crooked way, widely different from the straight way of the upright, ישרים yesharim, the straight in heart; they shall be led forth to punishment with the common workers of iniquity. Thus thy Church will be purified, and thy peace rest upon thy true Israel. Let him that readeth understand.  <chapter eID="Ps.125"/> <div eID="gen23076" type="x-p"/>

entries.d3529f12b3a13eaa540f6298d0b21c43e0f820c4: <div eID="gen10188" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Israel’s Bulwark against Temptation to Apostasy</title> <div sID="gen10189" type="x-p"/> The favourite word <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> furnished the outward occasion for annexing this Psalm to the preceding. The situation is like that in <reference osisRef="Ps.123.1-Ps.123.4">Psa 123:1-4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1">Psa 124:1</reference>-8. The people are under foreign dominion. In this lies the seductive inducement to apostasy. The pious and the apostate ones are already separated. Those who have remained faithful shall not, however, always remain enslaved. Round about Jerusalem are mountains, but more important still: Jahve, of rocks the firmest, Jahve encompasses His people. <div eID="gen10189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10190" type="x-p"/> That this Psalm is one of the latest, appears from the circumstantial expression “the upright in their hearts,” instead of the old one, “the upright of heart,” from פעלי האון instead of the former פעלי און, and also from למען לא (beside this passage occurring only in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.11">Psa 119:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.80">Psa 119:80</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.9">Eze 19:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">Eze 26:20</reference>; Zec 12:7) instead of למען אשׁר לא or פּן.
entries.4fb8c130bc253e9abd68d76244341cbe0d50b5b3: <reference osisRef="Ps.125.1-Ps.125.2">Psa 125:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10191" type="x-p"/> The stedfastness which those who trust in Jahve prove in the midst of every kind of temptation and assault is likened to Mount Zion, because the God to whom they believingly cling is He who sits enthroned on Zion. The future ישׁב signifies: He sits and will sit, that is to say, He continues to sit, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.9.8">Psa 9:8</reference>; Psa 122:5. Older expositors are of opinion that the heavenly Zion must be understood on account of the Chaldaean and the Roman catastrophes; but these, in fact, only came upon the buildings on the mountain, not upon the mountain itself, which in itself and according to its appointed destiny (vid., Mic 3:12; Mic 4:1) remained unshaken. in <reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference> also it is none other than the earthly Jerusalem that is meant. The holy city has a natural circumvallation of mountains, and the holy nation that dwells and worships therein has a still infinitely higher defence in Jahve, who encompasses it round (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.34.8">Psa 34:8</reference>), as perhaps a wall of fire (Zec 2:5), or an impassably broad and mighty river (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.21">Isa 33:21</reference>); a statement which is also now confirmed, for, etc. Instead of inferring from the clause <reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference> that which is to be expected with לכן, the poet confirms it with כי by that which is surely to be expected.
entries.5e7752746a3c0995d7f25e6666c7161df20bf23c: <reference osisRef="Ps.125.3">Psa 125:3</reference> <div eID="gen10191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10192" type="x-p"/> The pressure of the worldly power, which now lies heavily upon the holy land, will not last for ever; the duration of the calamity is exactly proportioned to the power of resistance of the righteous, whom God proves and purifies by calamity, but not without at the same time graciously preserving them. “The rod of wickedness” is the heathen sceptre, and “the righteous” are the Israelites who hold fast to the religion of their fathers. The holy land, whose sole entitled inheritors are these righteous, is called their “lot” (גורל, κλῆρος = κληρονομία). נוּח signifies to alight or settle down anywhere, and having alighted, to lean upon or rest (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference> with Joh 1:32, ἔμεινεν). The lxx renders οὐκ ἀφφήσει, i.e., לא ינּיח (cf. on the other hand יניח, He shall let down, cause to come down, in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.32">Isa 30:32</reference>). Not for a continuance shall the sceptre of heathen tyranny rest upon the holy land, God will not suffer that: in order that the righteous may not at length, by virtue of the power which pressure and use exercises over men, also participate in the prevailing ungodly doings. שׁלח with <hi type="italic">Beth</hi>: to seize upon anything wrongfully, or even only (as in <reference osisRef="Job.28.9">Job 28:9</reference>) to lay one’s hand upon anything (frequently with על). As here in the case of עולתה, in <reference osisRef="Ps.80.3">Psa 80:3</reference> too the form that is the same as the locative is combined with a preposition.
entries.156743d6cd6955208e20543f621552e18d70f8cc: <reference osisRef="Ps.125.4-Ps.125.5">Psa 125:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen10192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10193" type="x-p"/> On the ground of the strong faith in Psa 125:1. and of the confident hope in <reference osisRef="Ps.125.3">Psa 125:3</reference>, the petition now arises that Jahve would speedily bestow the earnestly desired blessing of freedom upon the faithful ones, and on the other hand remove the cowardly lit. those afraid to confess God and those who have fellowship with apostasy, together with the declared wicked ones, out of the way. For such is the meaning of Psa 125:4. טובים (in Proverbs alternating with the “righteous,” <reference osisRef="Prov.2.20">Pro 2:20</reference>, the opposite being the “wicked,” רשׁעים, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.19">Pro 14:19</reference>) are here those who truly believe and rightly act in accordance with the good will of God,<note placement="foot">The Midrash here calls to mind a Talmudic riddle: There came a good one (Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.2.2">Exo 2:2</reference>) and received a good thing (the Tôra, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.2">Pro 4:2</reference>) from the good One (God, <reference osisRef="Ps.145.9">Psa 145:9</reference>) for the good ones (Israel, <reference osisRef="Ps.125.4">Psa 125:4</reference>).</note> or, as the parallel member of the verse explains (where לישׁרים did not require the article on account of the addition), those who in the bottom of their heart are uprightly disposed, as God desires to have it. The poet supplicates good for them, viz., preservation against denying God and deliverance out of slavery; for those, on the contrary, who bend (הטּה) their crooked paths, i.e., turn aside their paths in a crooked direction from the right way (עקלקלּותם, cf. Jdg 5:6, no less than in <reference osisRef="Amos.2.7">Amo 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.23">Pro 17:23</reference>, an accusative of the object, which is more natural than that it is the accusative of the direction, after Num 22:23 <hi type="italic">extrem</hi>., cf. <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">Job 23:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.11">Isa 30:11</reference>) - for these he wishes that Jahve would clear them away (הוליך like Arab. <hi type="italic">ahlk , perire facere</hi> = <hi type="italic">perdere</hi>) together with the workers of evil, i.e., the open, manifest sinners, to whom these lukewarm and sly, false and equivocal ones are in no way inferior as a source of danger to the church. lxx correctly: τοὺς δὲ ἐκκλίνοντας εἰς τάς στραγγαλιὰς (Aquila διαπλοκάς, Symmachus σκολιότητας, Theodotion διεστραμμένα) ἀπάξει κύριος μετὰ κ. τ. λ.. Finally, the poet, stretching out his hand over Israel as if pronouncing the benediction of the priest, gathers up all his hopes, prayers, and wishes into the one prayer: “Peace be upon Israel.” He means “the Israel of God,” Gal 6:16. Upon this Israel he calls down peace from above. Peace is the end of tyranny, hostility, dismemberment, unrest, and terror; peace is freedom and harmony and unity and security and blessedness.  <chapter eID="Ps.125"/> <div eID="gen10193" type="x-p"/>

entries.b28ce6740f50247dac3f7e59057c0159b3791834:
PSALM 125
As the faithful being mingled in this world with the ungodly seem to be exposed to all the ills of life in the same manner as other people, the Prophet, comparing them to Jerusalem, shows that they are defended by an invincible bulwark. And if God at any time suffer them to be plagued by the malice of the wicked, he exhorts them to be of good hope. He however at the same time distinguishes between true and false Israelites, that hypocrites may not apply to themselves what is here said concerning the safety of the righteous.
A Song of Degrees.
Psalm 125:1-2
1. They who confide in Jehovah “are” as mount Zion, “which” shall not be removed, “but” shall abide for ever.
The supplementary words in this verse marked by inverted commas are taken from the French version.
2. As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so Jehovah round about his people, henceforth and for ever.
 
1. They who confide in Jehovah are as mount Zion. The present Psalm differs from the preceding in this — that while in the other it was said that the Church had been preserved by the power of God, without any human means, the Holy Spirit, in the one before us, teaches that in the time to come she shall always continue in perfect safety, because she is defended by the invincible power of God. When the Church is emblematically described by the situation of the city of Jerusalem, the design of the Prophet is to encourage each of the faithful to believe, that the safety promised in common to all the chosen people belongs to him. But in exhibiting to the eyes a visible image of the Church, he accommodates himself to the rudeness of those who, detained by the dulness of the flesh, still continue settled down in the earth. It ought then, in the first place, to be noticed, that to those who may not sufficiently apprehend by faith the secret protection of God, the mountains which environ Jerusalem are exhibited as a mirror, in which they may see, beyond all doubt, that the Church is as well defended from all perils, as if it were surrounded on all sides with like walls and bulwarks. Moreover, it is profitable to know what I have just now touched upon — that whenever God speaks to all his people in a body, he addresses himself also to each of them in particular. As not a few of the promises are extended generally to the whole body of the Church, so many contemplate them as at a distance, as far removed from them, and will not presume to appropriate them to themselves. The rule here prescribed must therefore be observed, which is, that each apply to himself whatever God promises to his Church in common. Nor does the Psalmist without cause make Jerusalem a representation of the Church, for the sanctuary of God and the ark of the covenant were there.
With respect to the explanation of the words, it is to be observed that the last two verbs of the first verse may be understood in two ways. They may both be governed by Jerusalem as the nominative. But some understand the first verb, לא ימוט al, lo yimmot, shall not be removed, only as spoken of Jerusalem and the latter verb, ישב, yesheb, shall abide, as referring to the faithful, so that according to this view there is a change of number, which is very common among the Hebrews — the singular number, ישב, yesheb, being used instead of the plural, ישבו, yeshbu. And certainly the sentence might not improperly be translated thus: They who trust in Jehovah, as mount Zion shall not be removed, shall dwell for ever, or continue steadfast, for the verb translated to abide is taken in this sense. We now perceive the meaning of the Prophet, which is, that although the world is subject to so many and so sudden changes as almost to put on a new face every moment, and although the faithful are mingled with and placed in the same external condition as others, yet their safety continues steadfast under the invincible protection of God. Not that they are permitted to dwell undisturbed and at ease; but because their safety being under the guardianship of God is assaulted in vain; at least they can never altogether fall, although they may stumble. But let us notice that the word הבמחים, habbtechim, which signifies, those who hope or wait for, conveys an implicit injunction to steadfastness of faith. Whoever, then, desires to be sustained by the hand of God, let him constantly lean upon it; and whoever would be defended by it, let him patiently repose himself under it. When God suffers us to be often carried hither and thither, or driven about like chaff by the wind, this comes to pass through our own inconstancy — because we prefer fluttering in the air to fixing our minds on the rock of his help. The similitude employed in the second verse is abundantly plain, teaching us, that as the continuous chain of mountains round about Jerusalem exhibits the appearance of walls, so God encompasses the faithful by his power, to ward off from them all harm.
From the mountains or hills which surrounded Jerusalem, the Prophet Ezekiel (Ezekiel 11:3) represents it under the image of a “cauldron.”
Similar forms of expression are frequently to be met with in the Scriptures’ God often promises to be a wall and a fore-wall to his people. But David, or whoever was the author of the psalm, proceeds still farther, showing under the figure of mountains the secret protection with which God defends his own people, to the end that the ignorant and feeble-minded who are still held down to the earth by their own dulness of understanding, aided by the sight of the mountains, may raise their minds upwards to the conception and contemplation of heavenly things.
Psalm 125:3-5
3. For the scepter
שבט If this word be translated rod, then we understand the Psalmist to speak of the assaults of the wicked upon the righteous; but as the lot of the righteous evidently denotes their estates, possessions, etc., שבט consequently seems employed as the emblem of dominion, i.e. scepter. This notion of שבט comports better with that of גורל[the word for the lot of]; and so the sense of the whole expression is, that the wicked shall not exercise dominion permanently over the righteous; the scepter of the wicked shall not rest,” etc. — Phillips.
of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the just, lest the just should put faith their hands to iniquity. 4. Do good, O Jehovah to the good, and to those who are upright in their hearts. 5. But those who turn aside into their crooked paths,
“Ou, se fourvoyent en leurs chemins obliques, ou, font fourvoyer.” — Fr. marg. “Or, go astray in their crooked paths, or cause to go astray.”
Jehovah will make them walk with the workers of iniquity. But there shall be peace upon Israel.
